answer: Style sheets (changeBox1/2 via setStyleSheet) go through Qt's CSS-like styling engine: each call re-parses the sheet and triggers a polish/unpolish plus style recomputation for the widget (and potentially cascades to children/ancestors depending on selectors). Before the window is shown, the widget isn't part of the live, laid-out render pipeline yet, so Qt can defer or short-circuit much of that work; once shown, the widget is actively painted, so setStyleSheet triggers real repaint scheduling and full re-evaluation each time, making it noticeably slower. changeBox3, which sets QPalette color roles directly, bypasses the style-sheet/CSS engine entirely - it's just a direct attribute write that Qt reads at paint time, so its cost doesn't depend on whether the widget is visible, explaining its consistency. This is a well-known QSS performance caveat: style sheets are convenient but expensive for frequent runtime updates, especially once shown. If you need fast, frequent color changes, prefer QPalette (or direct QPainter drawing) over setStyleSheet, and reserve style sheets for largely static styling set once at construction.

This usually happens when PyCharm doesn't recognize your folder as an actual project - e.g. you opened a single file instead of using File > Open and selecting the project's root folder, so no .idea project was properly attached and Settings has no 'Project: <name>' node to expand. Recreating .idea won't help if the project itself was never opened correctly. Try File > Open, pick the top-level folder containing your code (not a file), let PyCharm index it, then reopen Settings/Preferences - you should see 'Project: <foldername>' with 'Python Interpreter' underneath (in recent PyCharm versions JetBrains renamed 'Project Interpreter' to 'Python Interpreter', so don't search for the old label). Also check whether you're looking at File > New Projects Settings by mistake - that configures defaults for future projects, not your current one. If multiple windows/projects are open, make sure Settings is opened from the window actually containing your project, not from the Welcome screen, which only shows global settings without a project node.

askyesno and showwarning are two separate, independent functions in tkinter.messagebox - you can't chain them as msgbox.askyesno.showwarning(...). askyesno already returns True/False for a Yes/No dialog on its own: msgbox.askyesno('title', 'blahblahblah') pops the dialog and returns the user's choice directly. If you wanted a warning-style question box, use askyesno alone (it already reads like a warning question), or use showwarning alone if you just want an OK-only warning with no return value to branch on. So: input1 = msgbox.askyesno('title', 'blahblahblah'); if input1: ... Also, 'from Tkinter import *' with a capital T is Python 2 syntax; in Python 3 the module is lowercase 'tkinter', so if you're really on Python 3 that import should fail outright - double-check you're not mixing Python 2 and 3 examples. And prefer 'if input1:' over 'if input1 == 1:' since askyesno returns a bool, not necessarily the literal int 1.

Instance-attribute type narrowing based on which __init__ overload ran isn't supported this way - declaring self.stdin with different types inside separate @overload bodies doesn't work because attribute types are inferred from the single implementation's assignment, and pyright flags redeclaration. The typeshed-approved pattern (used by real subprocess.Popen) is to make the class generic: class MyPopen(Generic[AnyStr]) with self.stdin: Optional[IO[AnyStr]] declared once in __init__, then overload __new__ (not __init__) on the text: Literal[True]/Literal[False] parameter, returning MyPopen[str] and MyPopen[bytes] respectively (plus a fallback overload for text: bool). Callers then get MyPopen(text=True) inferred as MyPopen[str], so .stdin is IO[str], and MyPopen(text=False) as MyPopen[bytes], with .write() correctly rejecting the wrong type. This mirrors exactly how typeshed types subprocess.Popen's overloaded constructors and is the standard way to get argument-dependent generic return/attribute types checked correctly by pyright and mypy.

A few likely causes: (1) the element is inserted by JavaScript after page load, so find_element runs before it exists - wrap it in WebDriverWait(driver,10).until(EC.presence_of_element_located(...)) instead of calling find_element immediately; (2) By.CLASS_NAME only accepts a single class name, not a space-separated compound like 'a-size-small offer-display-feature-text-message' - use By.CSS_SELECTOR joining classes with dots instead, e.g. 'span.a-size-small.offer-display-feature-text-message', or By.XPATH with contains(@class,'...'); (3) Amazon frequently serves bot-detection challenge pages or region/locale-varied markup to Selenium's default (non-headful, flagged) browser, so the element may simply not be present in what Selenium receives even though it's visible to you - check driver.page_source for the text to confirm the real DOM Selenium sees; (4) the content could be inside a dynamically-inserted iframe you haven't identified - enumerate driver.find_elements(By.TAG_NAME,'iframe') and check each. Also, find_element_by_xpath is removed in Selenium 4; use driver.find_element(By.XPATH, '...').

The import statement needs a literal identifier, not a variable, so 'from name import *' won't work. Use importlib instead: import importlib; mod = importlib.import_module(name). That returns the module object from a string name (after your sys.path.append(d) makes it discoverable), working with your shutil.which()-based path discovery exactly as intended. To use its contents, either reference mod.func_name directly, or emulate 'import *' by pulling names into your namespace: globals().update({k: v for k, v in vars(mod).items() if not k.startswith('_')}) (prefer using the module's __all__ list instead of the underscore filter if it defines one). Note this globals()-dump approach is fragile since it can silently shadow existing names, so prefer mod.attr access unless you specifically need bare names. You could also use importlib.util.spec_from_file_location to import directly from a known file path without touching sys.path/PYTHONPATH at all.

'jupyter --version' and its extension checks reflect whichever environment's 'jupyter' launcher/core you actually invoked in that shell - typically your base/default env, not 'fastai' - regardless of which kernel a notebook is later switched to. Registering a kernelspec makes the fastai Python selectable as a kernel, but the notebook server (jupyter core, notebook package, extensions) can still be running from base. Inside a notebook cell running under the 'Python (fastai)' kernel, run: import sys; print(sys.executable) - if that's not fastai's python.exe, you're not actually running fastai's code despite the kernel name. If it is fastai's interpreter but 'import ipywidgets' still fails, check that ipywidgets and jupyterlab_widgets/widgetsnbextension versions are compatible, and that the notebook server itself was launched from an environment that also has jupyterlab_widgets (or, for classic notebook, enable the extension with 'jupyter nbextension enable --py widgetsnbextension --sys-prefix' from within the fastai env).

Python's reversed() only works on an object if it implements __reversed__(), or, failing that, if it implements both __len__() and __getitem__() (the sequence protocol), which lets Python synthesize a backward iterator by indexing from len-1 down to 0. If a class defines neither, reversed() has no way to traverse it backward and raises TypeError: '<ClassName>' object is not reversible. In your case, HBox (a container widget, e.g. from ipywidgets) apparently implements neither __reversed__ nor the full sequence protocol itself, so calling reversed() directly on the HBox instance fails even though it logically holds an ordered collection of children. The fix is to reverse the underlying sequence instead of the container: reversed(hbox.children) or hbox.children[::-1], since .children is typically a plain tuple that does support reversal. If HBox is your own class, add a __reversed__ method (e.g. return reversed(self._items)) or implement __len__/__getitem__ properly.

For a bilingual Totonaco-Spanish dictionary that runs locally as a static HTML page (no server), the simplest robust structure is: use Python (pandas/openpyxl) to read both Excel files once and export them to a single JSON array, e.g. [{'totonaco': '...', 'spanish': '...'}], plus a reverse-lookup view generated the same way. Build one HTML file with a search input and a results div, and embed the JSON directly as a JavaScript variable inside a script tag in that HTML (rather than fetching a separate .json file) - this avoids browser CORS restrictions that block fetch()/XHR on file:// pages opened by double-click. Add a small JS function that filters the array on each keystroke (case-insensitive substring match on either language field) and re-renders matches. This gives an offline, dependency-free, double-click-to-run dictionary. If the wordlist grows very large and filtering feels slow, consider a prebuilt local search index (e.g. lunr.js bundled locally), but for a typical bilingual glossary plain JS array filtering is more than fast enough.

Fixed lat/lon differences don't give a constant real-world distance because the length of a degree of longitude shrinks with latitude (and latitude spacing isn't perfectly uniform on an ellipsoid either), so you need geodesic math, not simple coordinate deltas. Use pyproj's Geod class: from pyproj import Geod; geod = Geod(ellps='WGS84'). Given a midpoint (lat0, lon0) and a bearing/azimuth in degrees, call geod.fwd(lon0, lat0, azimuth, distance_m) to get the endpoint exactly distance_m meters away along that bearing - call it twice, once with azimuth and once with azimuth+180, each using half your target length (150000 m for a 300 km line), to get two endpoints symmetric about the midpoint. Then plot those two points with ax1.plot([lon1,lon2],[lat1,lat2], transform=ccrs.Geodetic(), ...) - using ccrs.Geodetic() rather than PlateCarree ensures cartopy renders the true great-circle path. This lets you parametrize purely by center point, bearing, and length, with exact real-world distance regardless of map location.

Of your three options, the builder/factory pattern (#1) is the cleanest and most idiomatic - it mirrors exactly how the official docs test the Graph API: construct the graph/entrypoint fresh inside the test (or a pytest fixture) with an InMemorySaver(), so each test gets full isolation with no shared or global state and no dependency on internal methods. Prefer this. Option #3 (env-var-selected global checkpointer) couples app wiring to test configuration and risks state bleeding across tests, since the checkpointer is a single module-level singleton shared by however many tests import that module in one process - avoid it unless you truly need one production entrypoint object that must not be redefined. Option #2 (.copy() to override the checkpointer) can work as a pragmatic escape hatch when you must reuse an already-defined entrypoint without duplicating its logic, similar to FastAPI's dependency-override pattern, but since .copy()'s override semantics aren't clearly part of the stable public Functional API contract, treat it as a fallback, not your default.

Since both lists are the same length and already in corresponding order, zip them together and assign a new key per pair: for user, t in zip(user_data, available_times_array): user['c'] = t. This mutates each dict in place. If you'd rather build a new list without mutating the originals: user_data = [{**u, 'c': t} for u, t in zip(user_data, available_times_array)]. zip() pairs elements by position and stops at the shorter iterable, so make sure len(user_data) == len(available_times_array) beforehand - add an assert if you want to guard against silently dropping data when the lengths differ.

A very common cause of this exact symptom (predictions collapsing to one near-constant value) is applying Sigmoid twice: if forward() runs the output through self.sigmoid before returning it, and you then feed that into nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() (which already applies sigmoid internally to raw logits), you're squashing values twice - gradients through the doubly-saturated sigmoid vanish almost immediately, so the network stops learning and settles on whatever constant minimizes average loss. Fix: either return raw logits from forward() (no self.sigmoid call) and keep BCEWithLogitsLoss, or apply sigmoid in forward and switch to plain nn.BCELoss - never both. Separately, a sequence length of 2016 timesteps is extremely long for a vanilla LSTM; even with gating, gradients over that many steps tend to vanish or explode, independently pushing the model toward a trivial constant-output solution. Consider much shorter chunked sequences (or truncated BPTT), gradient clipping, and confirming your normalization doesn't collapse feature variance or the labels aren't heavily imbalanced.

Since your fastmcp Client already authenticates and calls the Cloud Run MCP server successfully, the missing piece is exposing that same tool to an LLM's tool-calling loop instead of calling it manually. The standard approach is an MCP-to-LangChain adapter: use langchain_mcp_adapters.client.MultiServerMCPClient with the same server config you already have (transport, url, headers/auth), then await its get_tools() - this introspects the server's tool schemas (name, description, input schema, exactly what you defined with @mcp.tool()) and auto-generates LangChain-compatible Tool objects with no manual wrapping needed. Pass that tools list into your agent, e.g. langgraph's create_agent(model=..., tools=tools, ...) or create_react_agent(...). Keep your existing Google id-token fetch logic exactly as-is for the auth/headers portion of the server config. The LLM then sees 'add' with its docstring/description and decides on its own when to call it with the right arguments; LangGraph dispatches the actual call_tool(...) against your Cloud Run server behind the scenes.

@tool captures the function's raw signature at decoration time, including 'self', turning it into a StructuredTool whose input schema then contains 'self' as a normal parameter. When the agent invokes the tool, LangChain supplies all schema-declared args as keyword arguments to the underlying callable - but since you're passing a bound method (self.read_file) as the implementation, Python's descriptor protocol already injects self as the first positional argument, so 'self' gets supplied twice: once implicitly by the bound method, once explicitly from the schema-derived kwargs, hence 'got multiple values for self'. Don't decorate instance methods directly. Instead, build closures inside get_tools() that capture instance state without exposing 'self' in the tool's signature: def get_tools(self): localdir = self.localdir; @tool def read_file(path: str) -> str: ...use localdir via closure...; return read_file; return [read_file, ...]. Now the tool's visible signature is just (path: str), with instance data captured via closure, avoiding the self-parameter conflict entirely.

bash_kernel is built on pexpect, which spawns the shell through a POSIX pty - something native Windows doesn't provide outside WSL or Cygwin. On plain Windows, even inside a conda env with Git Bash installed, pexpect's spawn typically fails or the kernel process crashes immediately after start, which Jupyter surfaces as the generic 'Connection failed / reconnecting' message rather than a clear error, because the kernel died before establishing its heartbeat. This matches your symptoms: the kernelspec registers fine (that's just metadata) but the kernel process itself can't actually run. bash_kernel's own docs note it isn't supported on native Windows. The reliable fix is to run it under WSL: install WSL2 with a Linux distro, create your conda/venv and install bash_kernel there, register the kernelspec from inside WSL, and launch Jupyter from that WSL environment (or point the kernel's argv at WSL's bash). Pointing kernel.json at Git Bash's bash.exe generally doesn't work either, since pexpect still needs a real pty that Git Bash's MSYS layer doesn't fully expose to Windows-native Python.

A single move_by_offset() jump (or one linear ActionChains sequence) moves the slider in one mathematically uniform motion, which is exactly the signature most slider-captcha anti-bot checks look for - real human drags have variable speed (fast start, deceleration near the target), small vertical jitter, and non-uniform timing between mouse-move events, often validated via a callback receiving the whole movement trace, not just the final X offset. To have any chance, break the drag into many small incremental move_by_offset() steps with randomized pauses and an easing-curve step size, plus slight y-axis noise, rather than one release. Note that Selenium's ActionChains can also be fingerprinted directly (navigator.webdriver, CDP artifacts), so sites with stronger bot detection may still block automated sessions regardless of movement realism. Also worth flagging: deliberately circumventing a site's anti-automation/CAPTCHA protection may violate its Terms of Service, so confirm you're permitted to automate this target before proceeding.

hello() calls the module-level logging.info(...), which writes wherever the root logger was configured via basicConfig() (filename='bandit.log') - not to your custom 'logger' object with the anomaly.log FileHandler, since that handler is only attached to the named logger you created inside logger(), not to the root logger. That's why nothing meaningful shows up in anomaly.log. Fix: create the named logger and its anomaly.log handler once, e.g. at module scope rather than repeatedly inside a function scheduled every second (repeated calls keep re-adding duplicate handlers), then have hello() log through that same logger object instead of the bare logging module: log = logging.getLogger('my_app') configured once outside the loop; inside hello(): if pyautogui.locateOnScreen('1.png', confidence=0.9): hello.counter += 1; log.info(f'Found 1.png, count={hello.counter}'). Also drop the redundant first try/except locateOnScreen call whose result is discarded - you're currently scanning the screen twice per invocation for no benefit.

A very common cause of this pattern: Trk.__init__ computes self.winwidth, self.winheight, self.width, self.height by calling win.winfo_width()/winfo_height() and canvas.winfo_width()/winfo_height() immediately after creating the widgets - but at that point the window hasn't been drawn/mapped yet (you call win.geometry(...) and win.mainloop() afterward in your main script), so those winfo_* calls return bogus placeholder values (often 1). Since coordinate() computes pixel positions using self.winheight captured at that broken moment, addText() ends up placing text at wrong/degenerate coordinates - often off-canvas or collapsed near (0,0) - instead of where row/col=6,6 should map. The manual canvas.create_text(...) call using screenwidth/screenheight works because those come from win.winfo_screenwidth()/screenheight(), which don't depend on the window being mapped. Fix: call win.update_idletasks() right after win.geometry(...) and before constructing Trk(...), or better, compute width/height lazily rather than caching stale values from __init__.

Your first pattern (calling session_maker() or session_maker.begin() fresh each time) is itself thread-safe and is the modern recommended SQLAlchemy style - each call creates an independent Session, so as long as you don't share one Session instance across threads/tasks, you're fine without scoped_session at all. scoped_session solves a different problem: it maintains a registry keyed by a 'scope' (by default threading.local(), i.e. current thread) and returns the same Session object for repeated calls within that scope, so code anywhere in that thread can call session_maker() and transparently get one shared, thread-local Session without passing it around explicitly - mainly useful for retrofitting older/global-style code (e.g. classic Flask-SQLAlchemy). You must call session_maker.remove() at the end of each unit of work to avoid leaking state into the next. async_scoped_session is the same idea for asyncio, but since there's no 'current thread' distinguishing concurrent coroutines, you must supply your own scopefunc (commonly asyncio.current_task). For new async code, explicit per-request sessionmaker() is usually simpler and preferred.
